title: A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health
script: Citra: [thoughtful] Bening, you cancelled your own check-up again, for the third time this year, to take your mother to hers. I need to say something about that pattern.
Bening: There wasn't really a choice. She needed the ride, and my schedule was the only one flexible enough to accommodate it.
Citra: [carefully] There's always technically a choice, even when every option feels equally unacceptable. What I'm worried about is that yours has quietly stopped including you.
Bening: I'm fine, Citra. Tired, obviously, but fine in every way that actually matters right now.
Citra: [reflective] You said something nearly identical eight months ago, before the exhaustion turned into that infection you let go untreated for two weeks.
Bening: That's not entirely fair. I was busy, not negligent, and those aren't quite the same accusation.

Citra: [honestly] I'm not accusing you of negligence toward your mother. I'm suggesting you've become negligent toward yourself, in a way you'd never tolerate from anyone caring for someone you loved.
Bening: If I'm honest, I don't know how to prioritize myself without it feeling like abandoning her, even briefly, when she needs so much right now.
Citra: [gently] I think that's the actual belief worth examining, that caring for yourself and caring for her exist in permanent, zero-sum competition.
Bening: I hadn't articulated it that plainly before, but yes, that's essentially the equation running underneath everything I decide.
Citra: [calmly] What happens to her care, practically, the day your own health finally forces the issue you're currently postponing?
Bening: It collapses considerably worse than a missed check-up ever would, presumably, since there's nobody else positioned to absorb what I currently absorb.
Citra: [encouraging] Then protecting your health isn't selfishness competing against her care. It's the actual precondition for that care continuing at all.
Bening: Put that way, postponing my own check-up starts to look less like devotion and more like a risk I've been quietly taking with both of us.
Citra: [seriously] I'll drive her next time, and you'll go to your own appointment that same afternoon. No further negotiation on this particular point.

quiz.question: What pattern does Citra confront Bening about?
options: Bening cancelling her own check-ups repeatedly to take her mother to appointments
Bening missing work deadlines
Bening avoiding her mother entirely
Bening spending too much money on healthcare
quiz.explanation: Citra confronts Bening about cancelling her own medical check-ups multiple times to prioritize her mother's care.

quiz.question: What happened eight months ago that Citra references?
options: Bening got a promotion
Exhaustion turned into an infection Bening let go untreated for two weeks
Bening's mother recovered fully
Nothing significant happened
quiz.explanation: Citra references how Bening's earlier exhaustion led to an untreated infection lasting two weeks.

quiz.question: What belief does Bening admit underlies her decisions?
options: That her mother doesn't need her help
That she has unlimited time and energy
That caring for herself and caring for her mother exist in permanent, zero-sum competition
That her own health doesn't matter to anyone
quiz.explanation: Bening admits she believes self-care and caring for her mother compete in a zero-sum way, so one must lose.

quiz.question: What does Citra ask Bening to consider about her mother's care long-term?
options: Whether her mother would approve
Whether her mother has other family members
Whether the appointments are truly necessary
What happens to her mother's care the day Bening's own health finally forces the issue
quiz.explanation: Citra asks what happens to the caregiving arrangement when Bening's neglected health eventually forces a crisis.

quiz.question: How does Citra reframe protecting Bening's own health?
options: As the actual precondition for that care continuing at all
As selfishness that competes with caring for her mother
As entirely unrelated to her mother's wellbeing
As something Bening should feel guilty about
quiz.explanation: Citra reframes self-care not as competing selfishness but as the precondition that allows the caregiving to continue.

quiz.question: What central claim does “A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health” develop?
options: Recovery after injury requires renegotiating ordinary independence.
Caregivers need care because responsibility can hide their own decline.
Longevity goals can obscure the quality and meaning of present life.
Rest after surgery can be disciplined care rather than idleness.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects the speaker’s reasoning and the limits of general health advice.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports the reasoning in “A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health”?
options: Practical limits persist even when a person appears improved.
The friends disagree over optimisation as a measure of a good life.
The friend notices strain that the caregiver has normalised.
The body’s recovery needs exceed the narrator’s urge to be useful.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects the speaker’s reasoning and the limits of general health advice.

quiz.question: Which qualification prevents an overconfident conclusion in “A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health”?
options: Adaptation is not identical to surrendering agency.
More years do not guarantee more wisdom or connection.
Progress may be uneven and should not be self-diagnosed from one day.
Support does not require guessing a person’s diagnosis.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects the speaker’s reasoning and the limits of general health advice.

quiz.question: Which response best expresses the speaker’s stance in “A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health”?
options: The intervention invites appropriate help and practical relief.
The narrator seeks support without treating dependence as failure.
The dialogue resists treating health as a competitive achievement.
The narrator accepts medically appropriate limits on activity.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects the speaker’s reasoning and the limits of general health advice.

quiz.question: What implication follows most clearly from “A Friend Intervenes on a Caregiver Neglecting Her Own Health”?
options: Care should make participation possible rather than demand normality.
Sustainable care includes attention to the caregiver’s wellbeing.
Health choices deserve reflection without promises of control.
Convalescence can require patience without romanticising illness.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects the speaker’s reasoning and the limits of general health advice.
